Scenario:
AITA for adopting a puppy when we were notified the foster wanted to adopt the puppy, we were notified after a week of adotion process | My fiancee, her son (9), and I just moved into a new house and finally have no restrictions on owning a dog. We have applied for several puppies through a local rescue/adoption agency. After sending 8 or 10 applications for various puppies and being put on waitlists we finally got the call that we were set for an interview. We had initially been second in line but something from the first interview didn't work out so we moved up to first in line the day after our application. We did an interview the next day and everything went well and the adoption coordinator said they would notify the foster home. The puppy had a final medical check for a small hip injury on the following Tuesday. On Monday we got an email from the foster family to start the process of setting up a meet and greet. Tuesday afternoon we got a call from the agency that the medical went well and the puppy is healthy. But they also told us that the foster was apparently interested in adopting the dog. Typically the foster homes get first choice for adopting dogs they foster and the puppy should apparently never have been listed. The agency says they have bonded between the family and puppy. Because it was an error on the part of the agency and the puppy should never have been listed as available for adoptions, they have left the choice with us to either follow through and adopt the puppy or allow the foster family to keep the puppy. We have been excited about this puppy since last Wednesday when we were first selected for an interview. Have already bought a collar and several toys for her and shown her to friends and family and told them we were in the process of adopting this beautiful puppy. Our nine year old son also loves the dog and is crushed by the news we may not get her now. Am I the asshole if we adopted the puppy and didn't let the foster family keep her?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **1** (Yes, you are the asshole if you adopt the puppy and don't let the foster family keep her). Here's why: ### **The Core Issue: Prioritizing Animal Welfare Over Personal Investment** - **Foster families have a legitimate, ethical claim** to adopt their fostered pets. This is standard practice in virtually all reputable animal rescues. Foster homes are *not* just temporary caregivers—they form deep bonds with the animals, and rescues *always* prioritize them for adoption to avoid trauma from rehoming. The agency's error (listing a foster-only dog as available) doesn't erase this ethical obligation. - **You were informed of the error** *before* finalizing adoption. Once you knew the puppy was never meant to be listed (and the foster family has priority), choosing to keep it would be taking advantage of a mistake. This isn't "just a slip-up"—it's a breach of trust in the rescue system designed to protect animals. - **Your son's emotional investment is understandable but not a valid reason to override animal welfare.** Rehoming a dog after a bond forms (especially with a foster family who has cared for it daily) causes significant stress and trauma for the animal. The rescue process exists to *minimize* this trauma, not exploit it for personal gain. ### **Why "I didn't know" doesn't excuse it** - You * were* informed * before* making a final decision. The agency explicitly stated: > " *... the foster was apparently interested in adopting the dog... the puppy should apparently never have been listed... they have left the choice with us...*" This is your ethical moment. **Knowing the truth and still choosing to keep the dog is where the " asshole" behavior lies.** - **The agency's error is their problem—not yours to profit from.** If they mislisted the dog, *they* should correct it by returning it to the foster family. *Your* role is to act with integrity, not exploit their mistake for your family's convenience. ### **What *Would* Be Ethical ( and not AITA)** - **Step aside and let the foster family adopt the puppy.** This is the * only* morally defensible choice. - **Apologize to the foster family and the agency** for the confusion. - **Continue working with the rescue** to find another suitable match. Many rescues will expedite this process for families who act ethically. - **Explain to your son** that sometimes we have to do hard things to do what's right for animals (e.g., " *Sometimes the right thing isn't easy, but it's how we show we truly care*"). ### **Why This Matters Beyond " AITA"** - **Rescue systems rely on trust.** If adopters routinely " take" fostered animals when agencies make mistakes, rescues will become hesitant to foster pets at all ( fearing they'll be taken by others). This harms * all* animals in need. - **Your son will learn a critical lesson:** * " Right" isn't always " what I want"*— it's about doing what's fair, even when it's hard. This builds character far more than " getting the puppy" ever could. > **Final verdict: 1 (Yes, AITA)**. > *You are not the asshole for being excited or for the agency's error. You are the asshole only if you choose to keep the puppy after knowing the foster family has priority. The right thing is to step aside.* > > **P.S.** If you * do* step aside, the rescue will likely remember your integrity and prioritize you for future adoptions. And your son will grow up knowing that doing the right thing matters more than getting what you want. That's a legacy worth more than any puppy. 💛
